name: Botox alternatives (Dysport, Xeomin, Jeuveau, Daxxify)

lead: Dysport, Xeomin, Jeuveau, Daxxify and Letybo are botulinum toxin type A products used like Botox to soften frown lines and other expression wrinkles, giving a smoother-looking forehead. They come from different makers and were approved at different times, from Jeuveau in 2019 to Letybo in 2024.

Each blocks the nerve signal to the treated muscle so it relaxes for a period of months. They are separate biological products whose units are not interchangeable, which is why the FDA gave them distinct names. Cosmetic registrations include comparisons in glabellar lines, while most published trials involve medical conditions such as cervical dystonia and limb spasticity.

paras: A clinician injects the chosen product into the target muscles, and results typically last about three to four months, with some products reported to last longer. Brands differ in onset, spread and dosing units, and people often choose one with their provider.

Reported effects include bruising, headache, drooping lids or brows and, rarely, spread of toxin (boxed warning). Antibodies can develop and reduce response over time. All are prescription products given by clinicians.

angle.text: Dysport, Xeomin, Jeuveau, Daxxify and Letybo relax targeted facial muscles like Botox does, so frown lines and other expression wrinkles soften. They share the same basic mechanism, and clinical trials support their use on glabellar lines.

lead: Several botulinum toxin type A products compete with Botox (onabotulinumtoxinA) for cosmetic use, mainly treatment of glabellar (frown) lines. They include Dysport (abobotulinumtoxinA, sold in some markets as Azzalure), Xeomin (incobotulinumtoxinA, Bocouture), Jeuveau (prabotulinumtoxinA, Nuceiva), Daxxify (daxibotulinumtoxinA) and Letybo (letibotulinumtoxinA).[1][2]

All act by temporarily relaxing treated muscles, which smooths the lines that form when those muscles contract. For appearance, the result is a softer-looking brow and forehead,, and brow-lifting with Dysport has been the subject of a registered trial. They are separate biological products whose units are not interchangeable, which is why the FDA gave them distinct nonproprietary names.[1] Typical cosmetic results last about three to four months, with some products reported to last longer.[1][2]

Brands differ in onset, spread, duration and price. Most published trials of these products involve medical conditions such as cervical dystonia and limb spasticity; cosmetic registrations include comparisons in glabellar lines.

paras: Botulinum toxin is a neurotoxic protein made by the bacterium Clostridium botulinum. It blocks release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction by cleaving SNARE proteins, causing a temporary flaccid paralysis of the injected muscle; of its seven serotypes, types A and B are used in medicine.[1] The toxin was first used therapeutically by Alan B. Scott in strabismus patients in 1977, and the product later known as Botox was approved by the FDA in December 1989 for strabismus, blepharospasm and hemifacial spasm.[1]

Cosmetic use followed quickly: Richard Clark's 1989 case report described treating forehead wrinkles, the Carruthers reported glabellar line treatment in 1992, and Botox Cosmetic received US approval in 2002 for moderate-to-severe glabellar lines.[1] The competing brands below entered later, and in 2009 the FDA gave the products distinct nonproprietary names (onabotulinumtoxinA, abobotulinumtoxinA and so on) to underline that dose units are not interchangeable between them.[1]

Dysport (abobotulinumtoxinA) is made by Ipsen and marketed with Galderma; its cosmetic brand in Europe is Azzalure.[1] Some accounts describe it as acting somewhat faster than Botox with more spread from the injection site, and a rough conversion of 2.5 to 3 Dysport units to 1 Botox unit is cited, although units are product-specific.[2] A double-blind study in cervical dystonia tested a three-to-one ratio of Dysport to Botox units, and a later crossover study examined the products' relative potencies.[3][4] Dysport was approved in the US in July 2016 for pediatric lower-limb spasticity in patients aged two and older.[1]

Xeomin (incobotulinumtoxinA) is made by Merz and sold as Bocouture in some markets.[1] It is named as a cosmetic neuromodulator, though the references reviewed give no cosmetic approval date for it.[2] A clinical trial of Xeomin in cervical dystonia has been published.[5]
Jeuveau (prabotulinumtoxinA) is marketed by Evolus and manufactured by Daewoong in South Korea; it was approved in the US in February 2019 for glabellar lines.[1][2]

Daxxify (daxibotulinumtoxinA) was approved in September 2022 for glabellar lines. Its pivotal trials, GL-1 and GL-2, enrolled 609 adults aged 18 to 75 at 30 sites in the US and Canada, who received a single injection of Daxxify or placebo.[1] Common adverse events listed include headache, eyelid drooping and facial muscle weakness.[1] Daxxify has also been studied in adductor spasmodic dysphonia in a phase 1/2 registration.[6]

Letybo (letibotulinumtoxinA) was approved in February 2024 for glabellar lines on the basis of three trials (BLESS I, II and III) with 1,271 participants aged 18 to 75 at 31 sites in the US and EU.[1]

Myobloc (rimabotulinumtoxinB, Neurobloc in the EU) is a type B product approved in the US in December 2000 for cervical dystonia, and is discussed in dermatology reviews alongside the type A brands.[1][7]

For glabellar lines, Wikipedia reports that smoothing is usually visible three to five days after injection, with maximum effect around one week and duration typically two to four months, sometimes six months or longer depending on the product.[1] Descriptions of cosmetic use say repeated treatment can shorten results or cause non-response.[2]

A 2017 Aesthetic Surgery Journal review traces the history of abobotulinumtoxinA over 25 years, and a Dermatologic Clinics review summarizes Dysport's cosmetic use.[8][9] Published head-to-head cosmetic outcomes between all brands are limited.

Adverse effects of botulinum toxins in cosmetic use include bruising, headache, flu-like symptoms, partial facial weakness and eyelid or brow drooping; spread of toxin from the injection site led the FDA to add boxed warnings in 2009 after warnings in 2008.[1] Antibodies that neutralize the toxin develop in a substantial number of patients receiving muscle-relaxant treatment according to an older laboratory study, and the authors noted this often necessitated ending treatment.[10] Descriptions of cosmetic use say repeated treatment can shorten results or cause non-response.[2]

Studies of these products are mostly in medical conditions. Randomised trials of Dysport covered upper-limb spasticity after stroke, hip adductor spasticity in multiple sclerosis and cervical dystonia.[11][12][13] Registered cosmetic trials include a non-inferiority trial of another abobotulinumtoxinA product against Dysport in glabellar lines (n=146), a trial of different injection volumes of Azzalure in glabellar lines (n=62), a small trial of brow lifting with Dysport (n=24), and studies comparing the muscle activity or field of effect of two commercial toxin preparations in wrinkles.[14][15][16][17][18] Published head-to-head cosmetic outcomes between all brands are limited.
The pivotal trials for Daxxify (609 adults) and Letybo (1,271 participants) were placebo-controlled single-injection studies in glabellar lines.[1]

Wikipedia notes that cosmetic use became widespread well before the 2002 US approval, and that a 1986 liability-insurance problem briefly interrupted the original product's supply for four months.[1] Brand names vary by region (Vistabel, Azzalure, Bocouture, Nuceiva, Letybo), and all products are prescription-only.[1]
